messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Security Guard
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rekha had always been the one who kept things steady. At sixty-six, she had spent decades as a security guard, her body accustomed to long hours on her feet, her eyes trained to notice what others missed. But nothing in her training had prepared her for the moment her younger brother, Arjun, was killed in a hit-and-run while crossing the street two years ago. She had been off-duty that day, walking with him after lunch. She remembered the exact sound — a wet, heavy thud that she still heard sometimes when a car passed too close. She remembered screaming his name, remembered the way her hands shook as she pressed her jacket against his chest, remembered the blood soaking through the fabric. She had tried to save him. She had failed.

In the months that followed, Rekha found herself unable to sit through family dinners where anyone mentioned an accident or a crash. Her husband, Raj, learned to steer conversations away from the news, from funerals, from anything that might set her off. But it wasn't just the big things. It was the way her stomach dropped every time she saw a dented bumper in the parking lot of the office building where she worked nights. It was the way she held her breath whenever she drove past a cemetery, her knuckles white on the steering wheel. She had stopped attending the annual memorial for her brother's death because the thought of standing near his grave made her feel like she was back on that sidewalk, the asphalt cold against her knees.

At work, Rekha had always been known as calm, even-tempered. But now she found herself tensing at the smallest hint of disagreement. When a coworker questioned her shift schedule, she agreed immediately rather than risk an argument. When Raj suggested they visit his sister's house, where someone might bring up Arjun's name, she said she was too tired. She had learned to keep the memories at bay by keeping her mind busy — by repeating the numbers on license plates, by counting the tiles in the break room, by pushing the images away before they could fully form. But the effort left her exhausted.

Her body had become a stranger to her. She woke each morning with her shoulders already tight, her jaw clenched as if bracing for a blow. During her patrols, she found herself scanning every corner of the parking garage, every shadow between cars, her heart racing even when nothing was there. The smallest unexpected sound — a door slamming, a horn honking — sent a jolt through her chest that took minutes to settle. She had come to believe that her body was permanently broken, that she would never feel normal again. What frightened her most was not the hypervigilance itself, but the certainty that she had caused all of this. If she had walked on the other side. If she had held his hand. If she had been faster, stronger, better. The thought circled back again and again: she should have protected him, and she had failed.

The worst moments came without warning. Sometimes, in the middle of a quiet night shift, the memory would hit her with such force that she felt like she was back on that street corner — the smell of exhaust, the sound of her own voice screaming, the weight of her brother's body in her arms. The memory felt more real than the fluorescent lights of the garage, more vivid than the security monitor in front of her. When it happened, she had to stop walking, had to lean against a wall until the wave passed, her hands trembling and her breath shallow. She had started taking longer breaks, hiding in the bathroom until she could compose herself.

What finally brought Rekha to seek help was a moment of quiet terror. Last week, during her shift, a car backfired in the parking lot. She dropped to the ground, her body acting before her mind could catch up. A colleague found her there, crouched behind a concrete pillar, unable to explain why she was crying. The next day, her supervisor suggested she take some time off. Rekha agreed, but what she did not say was that she was afraid to go home — afraid that if she stopped moving, stopped scanning, stopped holding everything together, the memory would swallow her whole. She came to therapy hoping to learn how to make the memories feel like the past, and terrified that she never would.
